It's nice to get a rough idea, but topography isn't factored in, nor is wind direction and speed. While wind direction wouldn't help out the folks near the blast (orange area), it would certainly help out those people further out looking at fallout. This website seems to be great at saying, "This circle of population won't be here, so long that it's all flat." Plotting Bismarck, North Dakota, and Denver, Colorado would offer significantly different results.

If we're hit, it's likely to be a first wave from subs right off our coasts. Expect nothing more than 2MT, and likely much less. Accuracy has increased significantly, so yields can be brought down for speed increase, and more devices with the same amount of fissile material. The follow up waves would be the older, bigger, ICBM's that were made decades ago.

If this website teaches you anything, it ought to be that blast radii vary for topographic and atmospheric conditions, and that if you honestly expect a blinding white flash, you probably ought to know where a fallout shelter is, even if it's just a sealed off basement (better than nothing). You'd have to stay there for weeks (once again to be determined by atmospheric conditions - rain will dramatically reduce the time needed to remain indoors, as was learned in the 50's tests).

The likelihood is really low that this would ever happen. We made it through the Cuban Missile Crisis, and all of the Cold War in the 80's without MAD. I think we're far more likely to face a financial crash, or meteor strike similar to what happened in Tunguska, in my humble opinion.
